pinboard.title: Can you use autoregressive diffusion to generate market data? (Jane Street)
pinboard.description:
The following is part of a series of posts about 2026 summer intern projects – for more, see “What the interns have wrought, special jumbo 2026 edition”

In quantitative finance we are used to models that take a stream of market data events for a given symbol (like resting orders being added to an order book, cancellations of those orders, executions) and predict that symbol’s future price. Generative models are less common. Imagine a model that could give not just a point estimate of a symbol’s price, but could actually synthesize book events—including the timing of their arrival on the exchange. You’d get price predictions, of course, but your rollouts would have hugely more texture than just that.

But what kind of data is market data? A generative model demands an answer to that question. Is it more like video, or text? That is, is it continuous or discrete? Market data seems to have features of both. An order book evolves via a series of turns as market participants put on, or take away, resting orders; there is no doubt a discrete action space. And yet, many of the most important parameters of a given order, like its price, have such a high cardinality that they basically appear continuous. Some simply are continuous: an easy one to overlook, but crucial for a generative model, is timing, as in “when does the new order arrive at the exchange.” Even that oversimplifies things. In practice the distributions are spiky: “pennying” (where you improve upon a price by one tick) is much more common than improving by two ticks, and orders tend to arrive in bursts, for instance around whole-number times.

One way to explore these complications is to treat your data as if it’s continuous and see how that breaks down. This summer, a research intern, Kavish, built a diffusion model for market data. Diffusion and flow-matching models are powerful tools for representing sequential, multimodal data in regimes such as image, video, robotics, and audio. Taking inspiration from Autoregressive Image Generation without Vector Quantization, Kavish created an event-level generative model of market data using autoregressive diffusion.

There were some technical findings along the way—for example, Kavish found that DDPM, while theoretically ideal for denoising in diffusion models, diverged, and that flow matching performed much better. But the headline result was that fully continuous diffusion did not lend itself to the jaggedness of real market data. Kavish’s various attempts to handle point masses via smoothing, on the one hand, and discretizing some of the model’s targets, on the other, have greatly clarified what an eventual generative model of market data might look like.

pinboard.title: Confessions of a Bad Texter - The Atlantic
pinboard.description:
We are truly sorry for our delayed response.
Whenever i receive a text, this is what happens. I pick up my phone. So far, so good. I experience whatever emotion the message elicits—the pleasant warmth of being reached out to, possibly the annoyance of being interrupted. Then, if conditions are right, if I’m not too busy or in the middle of talking with someone else, if my mind is at peace, if my anxiety is at no more than a low hum, if Mercury is not in retrograde, I will respond right then and there. If conditions are not right, it will be as though the text never existed at all.
Right now, I have 30 unopened texts. Scrolling through my messages, I find several more that I opened but forgot to respond to for anywhere between a few hours and a week and a half—from my parents, my sister’s fiancé, old friends who are accustomed to this kind of behavior, and new friends who are just beginning to be disappointed in me. At least two people texted me so long ago—more than a month—that to respond now and remind them how long they’ve been waiting would be worse than not responding at all.
I’m not proud of leaving people hanging. Every text I owe is a tiny siren in the back of my mind, blaring intermittent pulses of guilt. Unless I forget about it entirely, in which case I’ll remember it with a shameful jolt some days or weeks later. I’m not one of those modern hermits who thinks you don’t owe anyone anything, who likes every Instagram post she sees about boundaries and thinks that flaking on plans is self-care. I write about relationships for a living, and I believe that showing up for one another is the purpose of our existence. That’s, like, my whole brand. And so this is my greatest shame: I am a Bad Texter. I am slow to respond. I am forgetful. I get overwhelmed. My own mother has said I’m “probably worse than 90 percent of the other people that I text with.”
This might seem like a trivial pathology, but it isn’t. Texting is the currency of modern relationships. In 2024, Americans exchanged more than 2 trillion text messages, about 42 billion more than the year before, according to CTIA, a trade group representing the wireless industry. Some of those texts are probably spam. Some are advertising. Some are bits of automated busywork (click this link to confirm your appointment ). But many of them, hopefully most of them, are between people who know one another, reaching out for connection over the waves of the wireless spectrum.
According to a 2023 survey, texting is the No. 1 way that people prefer to communicate with their loved ones, beating out mobile-phone calls and absolutely crushing face-to-face conversations, which got only 8 percent of the vote. Texting came out ahead in every age bracket except the oldest; those 55 and older ranked texting and mobile-phone calls equally. No age group preferred anything over texting.
Yet at the same time, texting stresses people out. A third of Americans report feeling overwhelmed by the number of texts they need to respond to, and a majority say they struggle to keep up with their group chats. As Pranav Malhotra, who studies communication and media at the University of Michigan, told me, texting “is what the people want, but it’s not doing them any good.” And so, many of us end up feeling like Bad Texters. We are here, we are legion, and we are sorry for our delayed response.
Texting dominates our social lives like nothing else. According to the research firm Nielsen, American cellphone users started texting more than they called in 2007. Since then, unlimited phone plans and widespread Wi-Fi have removed many of the barriers that once led people to restrict their texts.
The ubiquity of text-messaging hardly seems worth questioning—it’s simply the way things are. But when you think about it, the modern predilection for managing all of our relationships by typing on a tiny touch screen is a bit odd. “For darn sure, it’s a lot faster to talk about things than it is to text them,” Naomi Baron, who studies language and technology at American University, told me. “Particularly if you have more than, let’s say, 100 characters’ worth to say. But it’s become the way of doing things.”

pinboard.description: The findings backed up what anecdotes and surveys have increasingly found in recent years: An overreliance on AI for answers erodes our cognitive fitness. When AI produces answers in seconds, we get used to that speed; anything that takes longer feels inefficient. And relying on AI also removes what the team called “productive struggle,” which can lead people to find their research strengths and passions.
